turns.q:
Your response was: "I mean... I looked through it. There were some parts that felt familiar, some that didn't quite. I'm not sure I'm the right person to say whether it all makes sense — it depends a lot on who would normally use this. I suppose some things stuck with me a bit more than others — there was more than one option, I think, near the middle of the screen, and I wasn't quite sure which one was the main one. Something about the way the options were presented felt a bit mixed up to me. I couldn't say much more than that without thinking about it more."

We want to understand what you meant by "something about the way the options were presented felt a bit mixed up to me", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The two buttons at the bottom of the screen — "Continue Shopping" and "Place Order" — are stacked in an order where the secondary action appears larger and more prominent above the primary action, making it unclear which one is the main choice.

B) The "Continue Shopping" and "Place Order" buttons are not grouped under any label or section heading, so there is no visual indication that they belong together as a set of options rather than unrelated actions.

C) The two bottom buttons are positioned at the same width and in the same layout area without any clear size or weight distinction between them in the wireframe structure, leaving their relative importance ambiguous.

D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to).

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: If I had to pick... probably A? I think. Though I'm not sure that's exactly it — it might be closer to another option, depending on how you're defining it. It's more of a general feeling than a specific thing. Other people might not even notice.

turns.q: What kind of work situation typically brings you to a checkout screen like this one?
turns.a: I'm not sure I have one specific moment in mind. It's more of a... recurring thing, I suppose. When the team needs to process something quickly and there's not much time for figuring out the interface. Though I'm not sure that's specific enough.

turns.q: When you looked at that bottom section of the screen, what were you trying to confirm about which action was the right one to focus on?
turns.a: I suppose just... complete the transaction. Confirm the order. I don't usually think of it as a 'job' — it's more like the last step in something larger. Getting it over the line without any detours.

turns.q: If the placement and sizing of those two buttons were redesigned, what would the layout need to show you at a glance to make it immediately clear which action closes the deal?
turns.a: 'Continue Shopping' was styled as if it were the main action — more visual weight, more presence on the page than I'd expect for a button that takes you backward. 'Place Order' — the actual thing I needed to do — looked secondary by comparison. That's the barrier. The fix: downgrade 'Continue Shopping' to a ghost button or a text link, something that reads as optional. And give 'Place Order' a solid fill color with real contrast so it's unmistakably the primary action. If those two things were right — 'Continue Shopping' quiet, 'Place Order' prominent — I'd have known immediately which was the right one without any hesitation.

turns.q: When you looked at "Place Order" — was it the color that made it fail to stand out, the fact that it appeared hollow or outline-only with no solid fill, or something about how little contrast it had against the background?
turns.a: 'Continue Shopping' should look like a secondary action — a ghost outline or just linked text, something that reads as an option for if you change your mind. 'Place Order' should look like a filled button in a distinct color — the kind that reads as 'this is the final step.' Right now they don't communicate that difference at all. That's the only fix needed.

turns.q: Looking at "Place Order" specifically — does it have a solid colored fill, or does it appear as an outline-only button with no fill at all?
